questions.q: What is (√5 + √3)/(√5 − √3) in simplest form?
questions.x: Multiply top and bottom by √5 + √3: (5 + 3 + 2√15)/(5 − 3) = (8 + 2√15)/2 = 4 + √15. Forgetting to divide by 5 − 3 = 2 gives 8 + 2√15.

questions.q: What is the converse of the statement “If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even”?
o: If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 4.
If a number is not divisible by 4, then it is not even.
A number is divisible by 4 and it is not even.
If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4.
questions.x: The converse of p → q is q → p: “If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4” (false, e.g. 6). ~q → ~p is the contrapositive and ~p → ~q is the inverse.

questions.q: Which of these functions is even?
questions.x: f(−x) = (−x)·sin(−x) = x sin x = f(x), so x sin x is even (odd times odd). x cos x is odd, and x + x² and eˣ are neither even nor odd.

questions.q: lim(x→0) (1 − cos²x)/(x sin 2x) equals:
questions.x: 1 − cos²x = sin²x and sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, so the fraction is (sin x)/(2x cos x) → 1/(2 × 1) = 1/2.

questions.q: A diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are all equal is called:
questions.x: Such a matrix is kI for some scalar k: a scalar matrix. The identity matrix is the special case k = 1 and the null matrix the case k = 0.

questions.q: f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² + kx + 5 leaves the same remainder when divided by x − 1 and when divided by x + 1. What is the value of k?
questions.x: By the remainder theorem f(1) = 2 − 3 + k + 5 = 4 + k and f(−1) = −2 − 3 − k + 5 = −k. Setting 4 + k = −k gives k = −2. Check: with k = −2, f(1) = 2 and f(−1) = 2.

questions.q: If (x + 5)/((x + 1)²(x − 1)) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 1)² + C/(x − 1), what is the value of A?
questions.x: x + 5 = A(x + 1)(x − 1) + B(x − 1) + C(x + 1)². x = 1 gives 6 = 4C, C = 3/2; x = −1 gives 4 = −2B, B = −2. Comparing x² terms, A + C = 0, so A = −3/2. Check at x = 0: 5 = −A − B + C = 3/2 + 2 + 3/2 = 5. −2 is B, not A.

questions.q: What is the sum of the first 12 terms of the series 1 × 3 + 2 × 5 + 3 × 7 + … ?
questions.x: The nth term is n(2n + 1) = 2n² + n. So S₁₂ = 2 × (12 × 13 × 25/6) + (12 × 13/2) = 2 × 650 + 78 = 1378. Leaving out the Σn part gives 1300.

questions.q: Ahmed and Bilal take turns rolling a fair die, Ahmed first. The first to roll a six wins. What is the probability that Ahmed wins?
questions.x: Ahmed wins on his 1st, 2nd, 3rd … turn with probabilities 1/6, (5/6)²(1/6), (5/6)⁴(1/6), …, a G.P. with ratio 25/36. Sum = (1/6)/(1 − 25/36) = (1/6)(36/11) = 6/11. Check: Bilal then wins with 5/11, and 6/11 + 5/11 = 1.

questions.q: Five horizontal lines cross four vertical lines. How many rectangles have their sides on these lines?
questions.x: A rectangle needs 2 of the horizontal lines and 2 of the vertical lines: C(5, 2) × C(4, 2) = 10 × 6 = 60. Using the sides of the small squares only (4 × 3 = 12) misses the larger rectangles.

questions.q: For a positive integer n, the value of ⁿC₀ − ⁿC₁ + ⁿC₂ − ⁿC₃ + … + (−1)ⁿ ⁿCₙ is:
questions.x: Put x = 1 in (1 − x)ⁿ = ⁿC₀ − ⁿC₁x + ⁿC₂x² − …; the left side is 0ⁿ = 0. Putting x = −1 in (1 + x)ⁿ gives the same. 2ⁿ is the sum without alternating signs.

questions.q: For every θ, sin⁶θ + cos⁶θ + 3 sin²θ cos²θ equals:
questions.x: With a = sin²θ and b = cos²θ, a³ + b³ = (a + b)³ − 3ab(a + b) = 1 − 3ab. Adding 3ab gives 1. Check θ = 0: 0 + 1 + 0 = 1.

questions.q: What is the exact value of cos 105°?
questions.x: cos(60° + 45°) = cos 60° cos 45° − sin 60° sin 45° = √2/4 − √6/4 = (√2 − √6)/4, which is negative as 105° is in the second quadrant. Using + between the products gives (√6 + √2)/4.

questions.q: On which interval is the graph of y = sin x rising throughout?
questions.x: sin x climbs from −1 at −π/2 to 1 at π/2. On [0, π] it rises then falls, on [π/2, 3π/2] it falls all the way, and on [−π, 0] it falls then rises.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 3, b = 4 and sin A = 3/5. What is sin B?
questions.x: By the law of sines, sin B = b sin A / a = 4 × (3/5) / 3 = 4/5. Inverting the side ratio gives 9/20, and 3/4 is just a/b.

questions.q: For x < 0, tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹(1/x) equals:
questions.x: For x < 0 both angles lie in (−π/2, 0), so their sum is negative; since the tangents are reciprocals the angles are complementary in size, giving −π/2. Check x = −1: −π/4 + (−π/4) = −π/2. The answer π/2 holds only for x > 0.

questions.q: How many solutions does sin θ + sin 3θ = 0 have in the interval 0 ≤ θ ≤ π?
questions.x: sin 3θ + sin θ = 2 sin 2θ cos θ = 0. sin 2θ = 0 gives θ = 0, π/2, π and cos θ = 0 gives π/2 again, so the distinct solutions are 0, π/2, π. Counting π/2 twice gives 4.

questions.q: Using differentials with f(x) = √x at x = 25, the approximate value of √25.1 is:
questions.x: dy = dx/(2√x) = 0.1/(2 × 5) = 0.01, so √25.1 ≈ 5 + 0.01 = 5.01. Forgetting the 2 in the derivative gives 5.02.

questions.q: If y = tanh⁻¹x (|x| < 1), what is dy/dx at x = 1/2?
questions.x: d/dx tanh⁻¹x = 1/(1 − x²), so at x = 1/2 it is 1/(3/4) = 4/3. Using 1/(1 + x²), the derivative of tan⁻¹x, gives 4/5; 1/√(1 − x²) gives 2/√3.

questions.q: ∫ x sec x tan x dx, for |x| < π/2, equals:
o: x sec x + ln|sec x + tan x| + C
x sec x − ln|sec x| + C
x sec x tan x − sec x + C
x sec x − ln|sec x + tan x| + C
questions.x: Take u = x, dv = sec x tan x dx, so v = sec x: x sec x − ∫sec x dx = x sec x − ln|sec x + tan x| + C. Using ∫tan x dx = ln|sec x| in place of ∫sec x dx gives the third choice.

questions.q: ∫₁⁴ √x dx equals:
questions.x: ∫√x dx = (2/3)x^(3/2), so the value is (2/3)(8 − 1) = 14/3. Leaving out the lower limit gives 16/3.

questions.q: The family y = A·e^(x + B), with A and B arbitrary constants, has a differential equation of what order?
questions.x: y = A·e^B·eˣ = Ceˣ with the single constant C = Ae^B, so only one constant is essential and the equation is dy/dx = y, of order 1. Counting two letters and answering 2 is the trap.

questions.q: The axes are translated so that the new origin is (1, 2). What does the equation y = x² − 2x + 3 become?
questions.x: Put x = X + 1, y = Y + 2: Y + 2 = (X + 1)² − 2(X + 1) + 3 = X² + 2, so Y = X². Check: the vertex (1, 2) of the parabola becomes the new origin.

questions.q: What are the intercepts of the line 3x − 2y + 12 = 0 on the coordinate axes?
questions.x: y = 0 gives x = −4 and x = 0 gives y = 6. Equivalently, the intercept form is x/(−4) + y/6 = 1.

questions.q: Maximise z = 3x + y subject to x + y ≤ 4, y ≥ x, x ≥ 0. What is the maximum value of z?
questions.x: Corners: (0, 0), (0, 4) and (2, 2), where z = 0, 4 and 8. The maximum is 8 at (2, 2). The point (4, 0) would give 12 but breaks y ≥ x.

questions.q: What does the equation 2x² + 3xy + 2y² − 5 = 0 represent?
questions.x: For Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + … = 0, B² − 4AC = 9 − 16 < 0, which gives an ellipse; it is real because the points with x = y = ±√(5/7) lie on it. B² − 4AC = 0 would be a parabola and > 0 a hyperbola.

questions.q: A vector OP has length 6, makes angles of 60° with the x-axis and 45° with the y-axis, and makes an acute angle with the z-axis. What is OP?
questions.x: cos²γ = 1 − ¼ − ½ = ¼ and γ is acute, so cos γ = ½. OP = 6(½ i + (√2/2) j + ½ k) = 3i + 3√2j + 3k. A negative k-component would make the angle with the z-axis obtuse.

questions.q: The parallelepiped with edges a, b and c from one corner has volume 12. What is the volume of the tetrahedron that has the same three edges from one vertex?
questions.x: Tetrahedron volume = (1/6)|[a b c]| = 12/6 = 2. Using 1/3 gives 4 and using 1/2 gives 6.

questions.q: A particle starts from rest with acceleration a = 6 − 2t m/s². At what time does it next come to rest?
questions.x: v = 6t − t² (v = 0 at t = 0), so v = t(6 − t) is zero again at t = 6 s. At t = 3 s the acceleration is zero and the speed is greatest.

questions.q: In Newton's law of gravitation, F = Gm₁m₂/r². The dimensions of G are:
questions.x: G = Fr²/(m₁m₂) = [MLT⁻²][L²]/[M²] = [M⁻¹L³T⁻²]. Multiplying by one mass instead of dividing gives [ML³T⁻²]; using r instead of r² gives [M⁻¹L²T⁻²].

questions.q: The second condition of equilibrium requires that:
o: The sum of all the forces is zero
The sum of the torques about any axis is zero
The body moves with uniform velocity
questions.x: The second condition is Στ = 0, so there is no angular acceleration. ΣF = 0 is the first condition; a body may satisfy both and still move uniformly, so rest is not required.

questions.q: Two stones are projected from level ground with the same speed, one at 30° and the other at 60° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, they have equal:
questions.x: R = v² sin 2θ/g, and sin 60° = sin 120°, so complementary angles give the same range. The 60° stone goes higher and stays up longer; the 30° stone has the larger horizontal velocity.

questions.q: A car speeds up uniformly from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ while covering 100 m. Its acceleration is:
questions.x: v² = u² + 2as: 900 = 100 + 200a, so a = 4 m s⁻². Check: t = (30 − 10)/4 = 5 s and average speed 20 m s⁻¹ × 5 s = 100 m. Using (v − u)² = 400 instead of v² − u² gives 2 m s⁻².

questions.q: A net work of 64 J is done on a 2 kg body that was initially at rest. Its final speed is:
questions.x: By the work–energy principle, ½mv² = 64, so v² = 64 and v = 8 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the ½ (2v² = 64) gives 4√2 m s⁻¹; forgetting the square root gives 32 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: The kinetic energy of a body of fixed mass increases by 44 %. Its momentum increases by:
questions.x: K = p²/2m, so p ∝ √K: √1.44 = 1.2, an increase of 20 %. Check: if p rises 20 %, K rises by 1.2² = 1.44, that is 44 %. Halving 44 % gives the tempting 22 %.

questions.q: A flywheel of moment of inertia 2 kg m² has an angular momentum of 8 kg m² s⁻¹. Its rotational kinetic energy is:
questions.x: ω = L/I = 4 rad s⁻¹, so KE = ½Iω² = ½ × 2 × 16 = 16 J (check: KE = L²/2I = 64/4 = 16 J). Forgetting the ½ gives 32 J; 4 is ω, not the energy.

questions.q: A small sphere moves through a viscous fluid in streamline flow. Its speed is doubled and its radius is halved. The viscous drag on it:
questions.x: Stokes' law F = 6πηrv makes F ∝ rv, so F changes by a factor 2 × ½ = 1: it stays the same. Taking F ∝ r² (as for terminal velocity) gives the wrong factor ½.

questions.q: When a body in SHM passes through its mean position, its energy is:
questions.x: At the mean position the displacement is zero, so the potential energy ½kx² is zero and the speed is greatest: all the energy is kinetic. At the extremes it is all potential.

questions.q: Two coherent sources vibrate in phase and send out waves of wavelength λ. Destructive interference occurs at points where the path difference is (n = 0, 1, 2, …):
questions.x: A path difference of an odd number of half wavelengths, (n + ½)λ, brings crest onto trough, so the waves cancel. A whole number of wavelengths, nλ, gives constructive interference.

questions.q: A car moves at 20 m s⁻¹ straight towards a high wall, sounding a horn of frequency 500 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. The frequency of the echo heard by the driver is:
questions.x: The wall receives f₁ = 500 × 340/(340 − 20) = 531.25 Hz and reflects it as a fixed source; the driver moving towards it hears f₂ = 531.25 × (340 + 20)/340 = 562.5 Hz (in one step: 500 × 360/320). 531.25 Hz is only the frequency at the wall.

questions.q: X-rays of wavelength 0.1 nm fall on a crystal whose atomic planes are 0.22 nm apart. Using Bragg's law, what is the highest order of reflection possible?
questions.x: Bragg's law 2d sin θ = nλ with sin θ ≤ 1 gives n ≤ 2d/λ = 0.44/0.1 = 4.4, so the highest whole order is 4. Using d/λ instead of 2d/λ gives 2; rounding 4.4 up gives 5.

questions.q: In a spectrometer, the telescope is used to:
o: Make the light from the slit into a parallel beam
Split white light into its colours
Bring the parallel rays leaving the prism or grating to a focus at its cross-wires, so the spectrum can be viewed
Hold the prism at the minimum deviation position
questions.x: The collimator makes the light parallel, the prism or grating disperses it, and the telescope focuses each parallel beam of one colour into a sharp line at its cross-wires. Its angle is read on the circular scale.

questions.q: Nitrogen has molar mass 0.028 kg mol⁻¹. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the difference between its specific heats per kilogram, cp − cv, is about:
questions.x: Per mole Cp − Cv = R; per kilogram divide by the molar mass: 8.31/0.028 ≈ 297 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Using 28 instead of 0.028 gives 0.297; multiplying by the molar mass gives 0.233.

questions.q: 2 mol of a gas with molar specific heat at constant volume 20.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is heated at constant pressure through 10 K. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the heat supplied is about:
questions.x: Cp = Cv + R = 29.11 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, so Q = nCpΔT = 2 × 29.11 × 10 ≈ 582 J. Check: 416 J raises U and nRΔT = 166 J is the work; 416 + 166 = 582 J. Using Cv gives 416 J.

questions.q: In Millikan's experiment an oil drop is held at rest by 400 V across the plates. It then picks up one more electron and is held at rest by 300 V, with the plates unchanged. How many excess electrons did it carry at first?
questions.x: qV/d = mg stays the same, so q ∝ 1/V: n × 400 = (n + 1) × 300, giving n = 3. Check: 3e × 400 = 4e × 300 = 1200e. 4 is the number after picking up the electron.

questions.q: An uncharged 2 μF capacitor is connected through a 500 kΩ resistor to a 10 V battery. The charging current just after the switch is closed and the time constant are:
questions.x: At the start the capacitor has no charge and no voltage, so the whole 10 V is across R: I = 10/(5 × 10⁵) = 2 × 10⁻⁵ A = 20 μA. τ = RC = 5 × 10⁵ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ = 1 s. Taking the current as zero at the start is the slip.

questions.q: Which of these materials has the smallest resistivity at room temperature?
questions.x: Silver is the best metallic conductor. Nichrome is an alloy with a much higher resistivity, germanium is a semiconductor, and glass is an insulator.

questions.q: A 6 V supply of negligible internal resistance is connected across a fixed 2 kΩ resistor in series with a light-dependent resistor (LDR). The output is taken across the fixed resistor. In bright light the LDR's resistance is 1 kΩ. The output p.d. is:
questions.x: Potential divider: V(out) = 6 × 2/(2 + 1) = 4 V. The 2 V is the p.d. across the LDR, not across the fixed resistor.

questions.q: A particle with charge-to-mass ratio q/m = 10⁸ C kg⁻¹ moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T. The time for one revolution is:
questions.x: T = 2πm/(qB) = 2π / (10⁸ × 0.1) = 2π × 10⁻⁷ s. Leaving out 2π gives 10⁻⁷ s, which is 1/ω.

questions.q: The wire of a standard resistance coil is doubled back on itself before it is wound, so that the current goes one way along one half and back along the other half. This is done so that:
o: The magnetic fields of the two halves cancel and the coil has almost no self-inductance
The resistance of the coil is halved
The coil stores more magnetic energy
The coil has a very large self-inductance
questions.x: In a doubled-back (non-inductive) winding the two halves carry equal, opposite currents side by side, so their fields cancel and almost no flux links the coil; its inductance is negligible while its resistance is unchanged.

questions.q: The self-inductance of a coil, in henry, is numerically equal to the emf induced in it when the current through it changes at the rate of:
questions.x: ε = L(ΔI/Δt), so L = ε when ΔI/Δt = 1 A s⁻¹. A steady current of 1 A induces no emf at all.

questions.q: FM radio reception is usually less affected by electrical noise than AM reception because:
o: FM waves travel faster than AM waves
FM uses a lower carrier frequency than AM
Noise mainly changes the amplitude of the received wave, and FM does not carry its signal in the amplitude
Noise cannot reach FM waves, which travel only by reflection from the ionosphere
questions.x: Electrical interference mostly adds random changes of amplitude. In AM the signal is the amplitude, so the noise is heard; in FM the signal is in the frequency, and the receiver can clip off amplitude changes. All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed.

questions.q: According to the energy band theory, a good conductor such as copper has:
o: Overlapping valence and conduction bands, so many electrons are free to move
A wide forbidden gap between a full valence band and an empty conduction band
A forbidden gap of about 1 eV between the two bands
An empty valence band and a full conduction band
questions.x: In metals the valence and conduction bands overlap (the conduction band is partly filled), so a very large number of free electrons are available at any temperature. A wide gap describes an insulator; a gap of about 1 eV describes a semiconductor such as silicon.

questions.q: A bridge rectifier made of four silicon diodes (forward drop 0.7 V each) is fed from a transformer whose secondary voltage has a peak of 12 V. The peak voltage across the load is about:
questions.x: In a bridge, two diodes conduct in series with the load in each half-cycle, so the peak load voltage is 12 − 2 × 0.7 = 10.6 V. Counting only one diode gives 11.3 V; counting all four gives 9.2 V.

questions.q: Light whose photons have an energy of 4 eV falls on a metal, and the stopping potential is 1.5 V. If the photon energy is raised to 5 eV, the stopping potential becomes:
questions.x: Work function φ = 4 − 1.5 = 2.5 eV. With 5 eV photons, K.E.max = 5 − 2.5 = 2.5 eV, so V₀ = 2.5 V. Scaling 1.5 V in the ratio 5/4 gives 1.875 V; using 5 − 1.5 gives 3.5 V.

questions.q: Besides position and momentum, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle also applies to the pair of quantities:
o: Wavelength and frequency of light in a vacuum
questions.x: The second form of the principle is ΔE Δt ≈ h: the energy of a state cannot be known exactly in a very short time. Wavelength and frequency of light are linked exactly by c = fλ, so they are not an uncertainty pair.

questions.q: The binding energy of carbon-12 is 92.2 MeV and that of carbon-13 is 97.1 MeV. The energy needed to remove one neutron from a carbon-13 nucleus, leaving carbon-12, is:
questions.x: Removing the neutron leaves a carbon-12 nucleus plus a free neutron, so the energy needed is the difference in binding energies: 97.1 − 92.2 = 4.9 MeV. 7.5 MeV and 7.7 MeV are the average binding energies per nucleon (97.1/13 and 92.2/12), not the energy for this neutron; adding gives 189.3 MeV.

questions.q: In a nuclear power reactor, the coolant (such as water or carbon dioxide gas) is used to:
o: Carry the heat from the reactor core to the heat exchanger, where steam is made
Absorb neutrons so that the chain reaction stops
questions.x: The coolant removes the heat produced by fission in the core and carries it to the heat exchanger, where it turns water into steam for the turbines. Absorbing neutrons is the job of the control rods, and slowing them is the moderator's job.

questions.q: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour warm the Earth's surface because they:
o: Absorb all the incoming sunlight before it reaches the ground
Let most incoming sunlight through but absorb and re-emit the infrared radiation given off by the Earth
Produce heat by chemical reactions in the air
questions.x: Sunlight (mostly visible, short wavelength) passes through and warms the ground; the warm ground radiates infrared, which greenhouse gases absorb and re-radiate partly back down, so less heat escapes. Reflecting sunlight would cool the Earth, not warm it.

questions.q: Aluminium reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂. What volume of hydrogen, measured at STP, is obtained from 5.4 g of aluminium? (Al = 27; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: 5.4/27 = 0.2 mol Al; Al : H₂ = 2 : 3, so 0.3 mol H₂ = 0.3 × 22.4 = 6.72 dm³. Taking Al : H₂ as 1 : 1 gives 4.48 dm³.

questions.q: 1 mol of a gas at 273 K and 100 atm occupies 0.20 dm³. Its compressibility factor and the main cause of its deviation are: (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; 0.0821 × 273 = 22.4)
o: Z ≈ 1.12; the volume of the molecules dominates
Z ≈ 0.89; the volume of the molecules dominates
Z ≈ 0.89; attractive forces between molecules dominate
Z ≈ 1.12; attractive forces between molecules dominate
questions.x: Z = PV/nRT = 100 × 0.20/22.4 = 20/22.4 ≈ 0.89. Z < 1 means the gas is more compressible than ideal, which is due to attractions. Inverting the fraction gives 1.12; Z < 1 linked to molecular volume reverses the cause.

questions.q: At very high pressures, the compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT of a real gas becomes greater than 1. This is because:
o: Attractive forces between the molecules become dominant
The molecules move faster at high pressure
The volume of the molecules themselves becomes significant, so the gas is harder to compress than an ideal gas
questions.x: When the molecules are crowded together, their own volume is no longer negligible, so the real volume is larger than the ideal value and Z > 1. Dominant attractions would make Z less than 1, the opposite effect.

questions.q: Ionic crystals such as NaCl are brittle and shatter when struck. This is because when one layer of ions is pushed over another:
o: The electrons in the crystal move freely and hold the layers together
Ions of like charge come face to face and repel, so the crystal splits
The covalent bonds between the ions break
The ions turn into neutral atoms
questions.x: A small shift brings Na⁺ next to Na⁺ and Cl⁻ next to Cl⁻, and the strong repulsion splits the crystal. In metals the delocalised electrons keep the layers bonded after a shift, which is why metals bend instead.

questions.q: In discharge-tube experiments, cathode rays can turn a light paddle wheel placed in their path. Textbooks take this to show that cathode rays:
o: Consist of particles with mass, which carry momentum
questions.x: Turning the wheel needs a push, i.e. momentum, so the rays were taken to be material particles with mass and velocity. Straight-line travel is shown by the shadow experiment, and the charge by deflection in fields.

questions.q: Which type of hybrid orbital has 50% s character?
questions.x: An sp orbital is formed from one s and one p orbital, so it is one half s. sp² has one third s (33%) and sp³ one quarter (25%). Choosing sp³ mixes up '50%' with 'four orbitals'.

questions.q: An ionic bond is most likely to form between atoms of which pair of elements?
questions.x: Potassium has a very low ionisation energy and fluorine a high electron affinity and electronegativity, so an electron is transferred to give K⁺ and F⁻. The other pairs are non-metals with small electronegativity differences and share electrons; carbon and chlorine is tempting because Cl is quite electronegative, but C–Cl is polar covalent.

questions.q: 210 J of heat raises the temperature of 10 g of a metal from 25 °C to 75 °C. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal?
questions.x: c = q ÷ (mΔT) = 210 ÷ (10 × 50) = 0.42 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; a rise of 50 °C equals 50 K. 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the value for water and is the reflex answer; 21 forgets the temperature rise.

questions.q: A plant makes sulphuric acid from sulphur by S → SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄. From 3.2 kg of sulphur, what mass of H₂SO₄ is obtained if the overall yield is 80%?
questions.x: 3.2 kg S = 3200 ÷ 32 = 100 mol, and each step is 1 : 1, so 100 mol H₂SO₄ = 9.8 kg in theory; 80% of 9.8 kg = 7.84 kg. 9.80 kg ignores the yield, 6.40 kg is 80% of the SO₃ mass (8.0 kg), and 2.56 kg is 80% of the sulphur mass.

questions.q: Which description fits a 0.001 mol dm⁻³ solution of hydrochloric acid?
o: A concentrated solution of a weak acid
A dilute solution of a strong acid
A dilute solution of a weak acid
A concentrated solution of a strong acid
questions.x: 'Strong' refers to the extent of ionisation: HCl is almost completely ionised in water at any concentration. 'Dilute' refers to the amount per volume: 0.001 mol dm⁻³ is a small concentration. Using 'weak' to mean 'dilute' is the common confusion.

questions.q: An aqueous solution is 20% NaOH by mass. What is its molality? (NaOH = 40 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: 100 g of solution holds 20 g NaOH (0.50 mol) in 80 g = 0.080 kg of water. Molality = 0.50/0.080 = 6.25 mol kg⁻¹. Dividing by the 100 g of solution instead of the 80 g of water gives 5.00 mol kg⁻¹.

questions.q: Given E°: Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V, Fe²⁺/Fe = −0.44 V, Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V, Ag⁺/Ag = +0.80 V. Which reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions?
questions.x: A metal reduces the ion of a metal with a more positive E°. For Fe + Cu²⁺, E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.44) = +0.78 V, positive, so it is spontaneous. The other three give negative E°cell values.

questions.q: For 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g), the concentration of HI falls from 0.80 mol dm⁻³ to 0.50 mol dm⁻³ in 50 s. What is the average rate of formation of I₂ over this time?
questions.x: HI is used at (0.80 − 0.50)/50 = 6.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. One I₂ forms for every two HI used, so I₂ forms at 3.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Forgetting the 2 : 1 ratio gives 6.0 × 10⁻³.

questions.q: A mixture of hydrogen and chlorine reacts very slowly in the dark but explodes in bright sunlight. Which factor causes the difference?
questions.x: Light energy splits Cl₂ molecules into chlorine atoms, which start a fast chain reaction (a photochemical reaction). Nothing else differs between the two experiments.

questions.q: Which period 3 element has the highest melting point?
questions.x: Silicon has a giant covalent structure in which strong covalent bonds must be broken, so it melts at about 1410 °C. Aluminium (660 °C) and sodium (98 °C) are metals with weaker metallic bonding; sulphur (S₈) is molecular.

questions.q: The thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases from MgCO₃ to BaCO₃. The best explanation is that, down the group:
o: The larger cations have lower polarising power and distort the carbonate ion less
The cations become smaller and more highly charged
questions.x: A small cation such as Mg²⁺ polarises the large CO₃²⁻ ion, weakening a C–O bond so CO₂ is lost easily. Larger cations further down the group polarise it less, so the carbonate must be heated more strongly. All are +2 ions and the carbonate ion is the same throughout.

questions.q: A sealed tube of brown nitrogen dioxide becomes much paler when it is placed in ice. This is because:
o: NO₂ condenses to a colourless liquid on cooling
2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄ is exothermic, so cooling shifts the equilibrium towards colourless N₂O₄
NO₂ decomposes into colourless N₂ and O₂ on cooling
Cooling shifts 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄ towards brown NO₂
questions.x: The dimerisation of brown NO₂ into colourless N₂O₄ releases heat, so lowering the temperature favours N₂O₄ and the colour fades. Reversing the direction of the shift is the usual Le Chatelier slip.

questions.q: The shape of the xenon trioxide (XeO₃) molecule is:
questions.x: Xe has 8 valence electrons; three Xe=O double bonds use 6 of them, leaving 1 lone pair, so there are four electron domains (sp³) and the shape is pyramidal, like NH₃. Missing the lone pair gives trigonal planar.

questions.q: Which of these ligands is bidentate?
questions.x: The oxalate ion bonds to a metal through two oxygen atoms at once, forming a five-membered chelate ring. NH₃, CN⁻ and H₂O each donate one lone pair, so they are monodentate even though H₂O has two lone pairs on the same atom.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of CH₃C≡CCH(CH₃)CH₃ is:
questions.x: The main chain has five carbons; numbering from the left gives the triple bond the lower locant (C-2) and puts the methyl on C-4, so 4-methylpent-2-yne. Numbering from the other end gives 2-methylpent-3-yne, which wrongly gives the branch priority over the triple bond.

questions.q: Ethyne reacts with one mole of hydrogen over palladium that has been partly poisoned (for example on BaSO₄ with quinoline). The main product is:
questions.x: The poisoned catalyst is too weak to hydrogenate an alkene, so the reaction stops after one H₂ adds to the triple bond, giving CH₂=CH₂. An active nickel or platinum catalyst with excess H₂ would go on to ethane.

questions.q: Ethene mixed with hydrogen is passed over finely divided nickel at about 250–300 °C. The product is:
questions.x: Catalytic hydrogenation (Sabatier–Senderens) adds H₂ across C=C: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃. Ethanol would need water, not hydrogen.

questions.q: Benzenesulphonic acid, C₆H₅SO₃H, is heated with steam in dilute acid. The organic product is:
questions.x: Sulphonation is reversible: C₆H₅SO₃H + H₂O → C₆H₆ + H₂SO₄ when water is in excess and the mixture is hot. Phenol needs fusion of the sulphonate with NaOH, a different reaction.

questions.q: Ethanol is heated with concentrated hydrochloric acid in the presence of anhydrous zinc chloride. The organic product is:
questions.x: ZnCl₂ helps HCl replace the –OH group: C₂H₅OH + HCl → C₂H₅Cl + H₂O. Ethene and ethoxyethane are dehydration products made with concentrated H₂SO₄, not HCl/ZnCl₂.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₂CH₃ is:
questions.x: In IUPAC naming of ethers the larger alkyl group gives the parent alkane (propane) and the smaller one becomes the alkoxy substituent (ethoxy) on carbon 1. 1-Propoxyethane takes the smaller group as the parent; 2-ethoxypropane and 1-methoxybutane are isomers with different structures.

questions.q: 0.88 g of ethanal is warmed with excess Fehling's solution: CH₃CHO + 2Cu²⁺ + 5OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + Cu₂O + 3H₂O. What mass of Cu₂O forms? (CH₃CHO = 44, Cu = 63.5, O = 16)
questions.x: 0.88/44 = 0.020 mol ethanal gives 0.020 mol Cu₂O (1:1). M(Cu₂O) = 127 + 16 = 143, so 0.020 × 143 = 2.86 g. Using the 2 Cu²⁺ as 2 mol Cu₂O gives 5.72 g; 2.54 g is the mass of the copper only (0.040 × 63.5).

questions.q: 3.7 g of propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH (74 g mol⁻¹), is exactly neutralised by 0.50 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. What volume of NaOH is used?
questions.x: Moles of acid = 3.7/74 = 0.050 mol; the acid is monobasic, so 0.050 mol NaOH is needed: 0.050/0.50 = 0.10 dm³ = 100 cm³. Treating the acid as dibasic gives 200 cm³; halving instead of dividing gives 50 cm³.

questions.q: The repeat unit of poly(propene) is:
questions.x: In addition polymerisation the C=C of CH₂=CHCH₃ opens, so the two former double-bond carbons form the chain and CH₃ is a side group. Putting all three carbons in the chain ignores that CH₃ is a branch; keeping the double bond is wrong because it opens up.

questions.q: A plant makes 80 kg of ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃ (80 g mol⁻¹). All its nitric acid is made from ammonia (1 mol NH₃ gives 1 mol HNO₃), and the acid is then neutralised with ammonia. What total mass of ammonia (17 g mol⁻¹) is needed?
questions.x: 80 kg is 1000 mol of NH₄NO₃. Each mole needs 1 mol NH₃ to make the HNO₃ and 1 mol NH₃ to neutralise it: 2000 mol × 17 g = 34 kg. Counting only the neutralising ammonia gives 17 kg.

questions.q: Nitrogen monoxide, NO, is present in car exhaust mainly because:
o: The high temperature in the engine makes nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine
Petrol contains large amounts of nitrogen compounds
Unburnt hydrocarbons react with water vapour
questions.x: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO needs a very high temperature, which the burning fuel provides inside the cylinder; the nitrogen comes from the air, not the fuel. Blaming nitrogen in petrol is the common slip; sulphur, not nitrogen, is the fuel impurity that gives SO₂.

questions.q: Ayesha wants to keep records of 500 library books and search them quickly by author or title. Which kind of application software suits this job best?
questions.x: A database program stores records in fields and lets the user search and sort them, for example by author. A word processor can hold a list of books but cannot search and sort records as a database does.

questions.q: Registers inside the CPU that a program can use to hold data and intermediate results of any operation are called:
questions.x: General-purpose registers hold data and partial results for many kinds of operation. The program counter, instruction register and MAR each have one fixed special job: next instruction address, current instruction and memory address.

questions.q: In a wave diagram of a signal, the height of the wave from its middle line to its peak is called its:
questions.x: Amplitude is the size or strength of the wave, measured as the height of a peak. Frequency is how many cycles occur each second, which is shown by how close together the waves are, not their height.

questions.q: In a busy LAN, the central hub is replaced by a switch. What is the usual result?
o: Less unwanted traffic, because frames go only to the destination port
More traffic, because a switch copies frames to every port
No change, because hubs and switches work in the same way
The LAN must start using IP addresses instead of cables
questions.x: A switch reads destination MAC addresses and sends each frame only to the right port, so other computers are not loaded with traffic. Copying frames to every port is how a hub works.

questions.q: A switch has 24 ports. One port is used to connect it to the router, and every computer uses one port. At most, how many computers can be connected to this switch?
questions.x: One of the 24 ports is taken by the router link, leaving 24 − 1 = 23 ports for computers. 24 would leave no port for the router.

questions.q: A Caesar cipher shifts every letter of the 26-letter English alphabet forward by the same number of places. Ignoring a shift of 0, how many different keys (shifts) can it have?
questions.x: Shifts of 1 to 25 each give a different cipher; a shift of 26 brings every letter back to itself, the same as shift 0. So there are only 25 useful keys, which is why a Caesar cipher is easy to break by trying them all.

questions.q: A teacher posts the link to her online class meeting publicly on social media. What is the main risk?
o: The video quality of the meeting improves
Strangers may join the meeting and disturb the class
The link stops working at once
questions.x: Anyone who sees a public link can join, so outsiders may enter and disrupt the class; meeting links should be shared only with the students. Posting a link does not change video quality or cancel the meeting.

questions.q: Buying a server costs Rs 120 000. Renting an equal server from a cloud provider costs Rs 5 000 per month. Ignoring all other costs, after how many months does renting cost as much as buying?
questions.x: 120 000 ÷ 5 000 = 24 months. Before 24 months renting has cost less; after that it has cost more.

questions.q: A model scores 99% accuracy on its training data but only 60% on new data it has not seen. What has most likely happened?
questions.x: An overfitted model has memorised its training examples instead of learning general patterns, so it does well on them and badly on new data. An underfitted model would do poorly on the training data too.

questions.q: A1 holds 7 and B1 holds 12. What does `=IF(A1>B1,A1-B1,0)` show?
questions.x: 7 > 12 is false, so `IF` returns its third argument, 0. The answer -5 would need the true part `A1-B1` to run.

questions.q: Text must flow down one narrow column and then continue at the top of the next column, as in a newspaper. Which feature does this?
questions.x: The Columns feature sets out text in newspaper-style columns that flow from one to the next. A table puts text in separate cells that do not flow into each other.

questions.q: A student may have several phone numbers, and all of them are stored under the attribute Phone. What kind of attribute is Phone?
questions.x: An attribute that can hold more than one value for one entity is multivalued (a double oval in an ER diagram). A composite attribute is split into parts, such as Address into Street and City.

questions.q: In a company database, Dependent (an employee's child or spouse) cannot be identified by its own attributes; it is identified only together with the employee it belongs to. What is Dependent called?
questions.x: An entity that has no key of its own and depends on another (owner) entity for identification is a weak entity, drawn as a double rectangle. A strong entity has its own key.

questions.q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
What does this query return?
```
SELECT Title FROM Book
WHERE Subject = 'Physics' OR Subject = 'Maths' AND Price > 500
ORDER BY BookID;
```
questions.x: AND is applied before OR, so the condition is Physics OR (Maths AND Price > 500): Optics and Mechanics, plus Calculus at 700, in BookID order 2, 3, 5. Applying OR first would give only Optics and Calculus.

questions.q: A Number field will store the population of each district, always a whole number of up to about 5,000,000. Which is the smallest whole-number Field Size that can hold it?
questions.x: Byte holds 0 to 255 and Integer up to 32,767, both far too small; Long Integer holds whole numbers up to about 2 billion. Double is for numbers with fractions, not a whole-number size.
An assignment is also an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = 4) stores 4 in x and gives 4; then y = 4 + 3 = 7.

questions.q: What is the C program called as the programmer writes it, before any translation?
questions.x: The program typed in the editor is the source code (source program). Object code is what the compiler produces from it, and the executable is made by the linker.

questions.q: Which file extension is normally given to a C source file?
questions.x: C source programs are saved with the extension .c. A .h file is a header file, and .exe is the executable made after compiling and linking.
The body runs for i = 2, 5, 8, 11, so c = 4. After the pass with 11, i becomes 14, the test 14 <= 11 fails and the loop ends, so i is 14, not 11.
dbl(4) = 8 is worked out first, then tri(8) = 8 + dbl(8) = 8 + 16 = 24. 12 is tri(4), which forgets that the argument was doubled first.

The inner brackets run first: r = 18 % 4 = 2, and the value of the assignment (2) is compared with 1. 2 > 1 is true, so 2 big is printed. 4 big wrongly takes the quotient 18 / 4 instead of the remainder.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of the Waterfall model?
o: Users can change the requirements at any time at little cost
Each stage ends with clear documents, so progress is easy to check
Users see a working part of the software every few weeks
Testing goes on from the first day of the project
questions.x: Waterfall finishes and documents one stage before the next begins, which makes it simple to plan and to measure progress. Cheap changes and frequent working releases are features of Agile, not Waterfall.

questions.x: `describe` is inherited from Shape, but `self` is the Square object, so `self.area()` runs Square's method: 3 × 3 = 9. No error occurs because the method is looked up on the object, not on Shape alone.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
print(min("pear", "apple", "plum"))
```
questions.x: Strings are compared character by character in alphabetical (character-code) order, and 'a' comes before 'p', so "apple" is the smallest. `min` does not pick the shortest string, and comparing strings is allowed.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
word = "banana"
freq = {}
for ch in word:
    freq[ch] = freq.get(ch, 0) + 1
print(freq)
```
questions.x: Each letter's count starts at 0 through `get(ch, 0)` and goes up by 1 each time the letter appears: b once, a three times, n twice. {'b': 0, 'a': 2, 'n': 1} forgets the + 1 on the first sighting.
g(0) = 0 and g(1) = 1, and each later value is the sum of the two before: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 for n = 2 to 6, so g(6) = 8. 13 is g(7), one step too far.

questions.q: A program checks the brackets in `( [ ] ( ) )` from left to right with a stack: each opening bracket is pushed, and each closing bracket pops its matching opening bracket. What is the largest number of brackets on the stack at any one time?
questions.x: ( push (1), [ push (2), ] pop (1), ( push (2), ) pop (1), ) pop (0). The stack never holds more than 2. 3 is the number of opening brackets, but they are never all on the stack together.

questions.q: In how many of the 4 rows of its truth table (for p and q) is (p → q) ∧ ¬p true?
questions.x: ¬p is true only when p = F, and then p → q is true whatever q is. So the rows p = F, q = T and p = F, q = F make it true: 2 rows. When p = T, ¬p is false.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
data = [3, 8, 3, 5, 8, 3]
print(max(data) - min(data), data.count(3))
```
questions.x: max − min = 8 − 3 = 5 (the range), and 3 appears three times, so `count(3)` is 3. 8 is the largest value alone, not the range.

questions.q: Which question does the Purpose criterion ask when evaluating an online source?
o: When was it published or last updated?
Who wrote it, and are they qualified?
Is it supported by evidence that can be checked?
Why was it written: to inform, or to sell or persuade?
questions.x: Purpose asks why the source exists, since a page written to sell or persuade may be one-sided. The date question is currency, the writer question is authority and the evidence question is accuracy.

questions.q: What does the passage mainly set out to explain?
o: which tunes tend to get stuck in the mind and a possible reason why
why radio stations should play fewer repetitive songs
what kind of music is played at weddings
how composers write songs that become popular
questions.x: It lists the features of "The tunes that stick" and then gives "a clue to why earworms happen at all". Radio and weddings are only places where a tune might be heard.

questions.q: Which feature of tunes that stick is mentioned in the passage?
o: A simple, predictable pattern with one small surprise
questions.x: The second paragraph describes a melody "the ear can predict, yet with one small surprise". The tunes are "usually simple", so a complicated melody is the opposite.

questions.q: If the explanation in the third paragraph is right, which of these would be least likely to get stuck in the mind?
o: A simple chorus heard many times on the radio
A catchy tune with one unexpected note
A few lines of a song that stop in the middle
A long, complex piece heard once all the way to its end
questions.x: Tunes that stick are simple, repeated and unfinished; a complex piece heard once and "to the end" has none of these features, and finishing a song makes the loop "more likely to stop". A fragment that stops in the middle is exactly what the passage says sticks.

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "resolving" most nearly means:
o: coming to a settled, finished close
questions.x: The fragment is one of "a few lines that stop without resolving", later called "unfinished", "like a question without an answer". Making a firm decision is the commoner meaning, used of people.

questions.q: At the start of the third paragraph, the words "That last feature" refer to:
o: the repetition of a chorus many times
the unexpected note in a simple tune
the clear rhythm of the melody
the fact that it is often an unfinished fragment that sticks
questions.x: The last feature named in the second paragraph is that "a fragment rather than a whole song" sticks, "a few lines that stop without resolving"; the third paragraph then discusses the unfinished. The surprise note was mentioned earlier.

questions.q: The passage is mainly an argument for:
o: choosing quiet people rather than talkative ones as leaders
arranging discussions so that both quick speakers and quiet thinkers are heard
doing class projects alone instead of in groups
asking talkative people to stay silent in meetings
questions.x: The writer proposes "a simple change" so that a group "hears from everyone it has gathered". Silencing talkers is rejected: "The point is not to silence the talkers."

questions.q: What does the writer suggest a group should do before anyone speaks?
o: Let the most confident member speak first
Have everyone write down their ideas privately for a few minutes
Vote on which idea is best
Split into a group of talkers and a group of thinkers
questions.x: The third paragraph says "everyone writes down their ideas privately for five minutes before anyone speaks". Letting the confident speak first is the present pattern the writer wants to change.

questions.q: The passage suggests that a group made up only of people who think out loud would most likely:
o: reach better decisions than a mixed group
miss some mistakes that quieter thinkers would have caught
take longer than any other group to decide
questions.x: "Each catches mistakes that the other misses", so a group with only one style would miss the mistakes the other style catches. Better decisions than a mixed group goes against "Neither style is superior".

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "sharpens" most nearly means:
o: makes their thinking clearer and quicker
questions.x: Out-loud thinkers "need to hear an idea spoken before they can judge it", so argument improves their thinking. Giving something a pointed edge is the literal meaning, used for knives.

questions.q: The writer's view of the two ways of working is best described as:
o: strongly in favour of quiet thinkers
dismissive of people who think out loud
unsure whether either has any value
questions.x: The writer says "Neither style is superior; each catches mistakes that the other misses." Wanting quiet thinkers heard is about fairness, not preferring them: "The point is not to silence the talkers."
